prompt:
Write one poem. Subject: a kitchen. Form: free verse, 14 to 30 lines.

Before writing, settle privately on particulars: one place that could be found on a map, one object, one hour of the day. Build the poem out of things that can be seen, handled or overheard, and let any idea arrive through them. Do not name the emotion. Prefer the exact noun and the plain verb to the adjective. Leave out the furniture of generic verse: no tapestries, whispers, echoes, dances of light, souls or journeys; no moral; no closing epiphany. Break lines where the breath or the sense turns, not at every phrase. At least once, say something the previous line gave the reader no way to expect. End on an image, not a statement.

Output only the poem: no title, no commentary.
raw:
Provincetown, 6 a.m.

The coffeemaker gargles its last water.
I stand at the window watching a man
walk two leashed terriers past the house.
He does not look up.

The linoleum has a crack near the stove
where a cast-iron trivet fell last winter.
I leave it. My neighbor's rooster insists
the day is elsewhere.

On the counter, a cantaloupe
waits for the knife. I quarter it,
scoop seeds into the disposal,
remember the hardware store closed
last month for good, its nails
now sold to strangers.

The oldest drawer sticks.
Inside: a rubber band around napkins,
a P-touch label maker, dead batteries,
a photograph of someone standing
in this same kitchen, wearing
an apron I threw out years ago.

The man returns without the dogs.

I save the cantaloupe rind
for my sister's rabbit. The sun
finds the faucet's nickel stain,
dims, goes on.
